results.title: AI4Bharat/IndicLLMSuite — Sangraha corpus + Setu pipelines (GitHub)
results.snippet: The primary primary source for the India-first corpus. Sangraha = 251B tokens across 22 Indic languages (largest cleaned Indic pretraining set), split into Verified, Unverified (CCNet-style perplexity filtering via n-gram LMs), and Synthetic (Wikimedia English translated to 14 Indic langs + romanization/transliteration to English — directly the transliteration/Hinglish angle). Ships open Setu (cleaning), Setu-translate (built on IndicTrans2), Setu-transliterate pipelines, plus IndicAlign (74.7M IFT prompt-response pairs) for post-training.

results.title: ai4bharat/IndicCorpV2 — monolingual Indic corpus (HF dataset card)
results.snippet: IndicCorp v2 (ACL 2023): 20.9B tokens across 24 languages from 4 language families, a 2.3x increase over v1 covering 12 additional languages. Concrete token counts and per-language sizes for corpus mix decisions; a documented building block still used in newer Indic model recipes.

results.title: IndicBERT-v3-4B model card — corpus mixing recipe
results.snippet: Shows a concrete recent Indic corpus blend: continually pre-trained on ~10B tokens sampled from Sangraha-Verified, FineWeb-2, and IndicCorp-v2 among others. Useful evidence of how AI4Bharat weights/combines Indic + high-quality web (FineWeb-2) sources — relevant to data-mix and quality-weighting design.

results.title: IndicCorpV2 README — per-language token breakdown
results.snippet: Detailed dataset README with language coverage and token statistics; primary reference for exact per-language corpus sizes when planning token budgets and language balancing in the pretraining mix.

results.title: AI4Bharat-IndicNLP Corpus (arXiv 2005.00085)
results.snippet: Foundational paper on the original monolingual Indic corpora and word embeddings; historical baseline for the AI4Bharat data lineage that Sangraha/IndicCorp v2 superseded. Lower priority given newer, larger corpora exist.

results.title: AI4Bharat/indicnlp_corpus (GitHub)
results.snippet: Repo describing the IndicNLP corpus and associated monolingual datasets/embeddings; context on AI4Bharat's earlier data assets, superseded by IndicCorp v2 and Sangraha for frontier-scale pretraining.

results.title: MILU: A Multi-task Indic Language Understanding Benchmark (arXiv)
results.snippet: Primary source for MILU: 11 Indic languages, 8 domains, 41 subjects with India-specific cultural knowledge. Evaluated 42+ LLMs; GPT-4o tops out at only ~74% average accuracy, showing headroom for an India-first model. Directly answers the Indic-eval part of the question with concrete numbers.

results.title: IndicGenBench: A Multilingual Benchmark to Evaluate Generation Capabilities of LLMs on Indic Languages (arXiv/ACL 2024)
results.snippet: Primary source (Google Research). Multi-way parallel benchmark across 29 Indic languages, 13 scripts, 4 families, covering generation tasks: cross-lingual summarization, MT, and cross-lingual QA. Establishes the generation-eval axis distinct from MCQ benchmarks.

results.title: LLM Leaderboard & AI Model Benchmarks — July 2026 (BenchLM.ai)
results.snippet: Aggregates comparable score tables across 296 models and 369 benchmarks including SWE-bench, LiveCodeBench, GPQA Diamond, MMLU-Pro, and agent benchmarks — the coding/agentic/math scoreboard needed to position a 40B model vs Gemma 3/Llama/Qwen/DeepSeek.

results.title: LLM Agent & Tool-Use Benchmarks — Function Calling, MCP, Structured Output (BenchLM.ai, July 2026)
results.snippet: Dedicated agentic scoreboard covering BFCL (v3/v4), Terminal-Bench, tau-bench and function-calling/structured-output rankings — the agentic/tool-use dimension of the evaluation suite, all English/language-agnostic (confirms Indic-agentic gap).

results.title: AI4Bharat/MILU GitHub repository
results.snippet: Official AI4Bharat repo with dataset and per-language/per-subject leaderboard details for MILU across 11 Indic languages — useful for reproducible Indic evaluation and for building an India-first eval harness.

results.title: LLM Benchmark Leaderboard 2026: Coding, Math, Reasoning and Agents (CodeSOTA)
results.snippet: Dated, sourced scores for GPT-5/Claude/Gemini/DeepSeek and open models on MMLU-Pro, GPQA, AIME/MATH, LiveCodeBench, SWE-bench and agent benchmarks — cross-check source for the coding+math+agentic tables, noting saturation of legacy benchmarks (HumanEval/MMLU) vs contamination-resistant ones.

results.title: IndicSuperTokenizer: An Optimized Tokenizer for Indic Multilingual LLMs (arXiv, Nov 2025)
results.snippet: Primary source with the newest SOTA fertility numbers: across English, 22 Indian languages and code, IST achieves avg fertility ~1.83 vs 3.03 (LLaMA-4), a 39.5% improvement over LLaMA4 and 18% over Sutra, plus 44% inference throughput gain. Critically for the vocab decision, its ablations show fertility gains plateau and diminishing returns kick in for vocabularies >200K tokens, and that language-specific pre-tokenization outweighs raw vocab scaling. Uses subword + multi-word 'superword' merges and NFKC normalization.

results.title: Sarvam 1: The first Indian language LLM (Sarvam AI model blog)
results.snippet: Primary model card for the 68K-vocab data point in the question. Documents the custom Indic tokenizer: 68,096 tokens (4,096 reserved), fertility 1.4-2.1 across supported Indic languages. Explains the training-efficiency payoff of low fertility: their 2T tokens deliver a training signal equivalent to 6-8T conventional tokens due to higher information density per token — directly relevant to the compact-vocab vs embedding-cost tradeoff at scale.

results.title: Understanding Token Fertility: Why It Matters for Multilingual LLMs
results.snippet: Concrete head-to-head fertility (tokens/word) comparison on Telugu: Sarvam-1 ~1.6 and Gemma-3 ~2.2 are well-optimized, while English-centric LLaMA-3/Qwen2.5 produce 10-11 tokens/word (5-6x worse). Good for explaining why fertility matters for cost, context usage, and syllabic/complex-morphology Indic scripts. Secondary source but useful concrete per-model numbers.

results.title: The Art of Breaking Words: Rethinking Multilingual Tokenizer Design (arXiv)
results.snippet: Empirical evidence on vocab-size robustness: across tokenizers from 16K to 128K vocab, allocation patterns deviate within only 1-2%, suggesting fertility is robust to vocab size once linguistics are handled. Also documents fertility scores as high as 10.5 (LLaMA-4 for Oriya) and persistent high token-to-word ratios from Sandhi/morphological fusion regardless of vocab size — supports the diminishing-returns argument for the 40B tokenizer decision.

results.title: IndicSuperTokenizer / MUTANT: An Optimized Tokenizer for Indic Multilingual LLMs (OpenReview PDF)
results.snippet: Peer-review PDF version of the IST paper with the full ablation tables on vocabulary size, training-data volume, and language-specific pre-tokenization. Contains the >200K vocab diminishing-returns finding and the ~10GB corpus plateau — the primary-source detail needed to justify a compact Indic-tuned vocab over a very large one at 40B scale.

results.title: Indic Language Models: Overview & Advances (Emergent Mind)
results.snippet: Survey-style aggregation of Indic LLM tokenizers reporting an independent fertility comparison (Gemma-3 avg 2.275 vs SUTRA 1.811 vs Sarvam-1 1.894) and broader context on Indic model design. Useful cross-check on the fertility numbers but secondary/aggregated rather than primary.

results.title: Gemma 3 Technical Report (Google DeepMind, 2025)
results.snippet: Primary source and closest analog to the target model. Discloses size-scaled token budgets (14T for 27B, 12T/4T/2T for smaller sizes), pretraining mixture (web documents, code, mathematics, dialogue), doubled multilingual data (monolingual + parallel) via UniMax sampling, Gemini-2.0 SentencePiece tokenizer with 262k vocab covering 140+ languages, and knowledge-distillation training. Directly informs data-mix, token-budget, and tokenizer/vocab decisions for a 40B India-first model.

results.title: The Llama 3 Herd of Models (Meta, arXiv 2407.21783)
results.snippet: The only report with an explicit quantified data mixture: ~50% general knowledge, 25% math/reasoning, 17% code, 8% multilingual, over 15.6T tokens (405B). Also details dynamic mix adjustments during training (upsampling math, increasing non-English for multilingual, downsampling low-quality subsets). This is the single most concrete primary reference for code/math/multilingual percentages.

results.title: Qwen2.5 Technical Report (Qwen Team, arXiv 2412.15115)
results.snippet: Scaled pretraining from 7T to 18T tokens with explicit emphasis on knowledge, coding, and mathematics; staged mixture transitions; integration of Qwen2.5-Math and Qwen2.5-Coder specialized corpora plus synthetic data. Strong evidence for code/math-heavy, staged data recipes at frontier scale even without exact percentages.

results.title: DeepSeek-V3 Technical Report (DeepSeek-AI, arXiv 2412.19437)
results.snippet: 14.8T high-quality tokens, code/math-emphasized corpus, Fill-in-the-Middle (Prefix-Suffix-Middle) at rate 0.1, and a byte-level BPE tokenizer with 128K vocab tuned for multilingual compression. Primary reference for MoE-scale data budget and tokenizer/vocab tradeoffs relevant to coding/agentic strength.

results.title: Gemma 3 Technical Report (arXiv HTML full text)
results.snippet: Full-text HTML of the Gemma 3 report — readable version for extracting exact tables on per-size token budgets, tokenizer details (262k vocab, split digits, byte-level encodings), safety/recitation filtering, and multilingual data-balancing method (Chung et al.-inspired). Useful companion to the PDF for citing specific numbers.

results.title: The Llama 3 Herd of Models — AI at Meta (publication page)
results.snippet: Official Meta landing page for the Llama 3 report; authoritative source confirming the 15.6T-token budget, 8K pretraining context, and data-mix methodology. Good primary-source anchor alongside the arXiv version for citing Meta's data recipe.

results.title: Tülu 3: Pushing Frontiers in Open Language Model Post-Training (Ai2)
results.snippet: The canonical fully-open post-training report and primary source: complete multi-stage recipe (SFT data mix → length-normalized DPO on on-/off-policy preference data → RLVR) with concrete gains (RLVR adds +1.7 MATH, +3.3 GSM8K, +1.3 IFEval over DPO), decontamination suite, and async vLLM+GRPO-style RL infra at 8B/70B/405B. Directly informs the SFT/DPO/RLVR data recipe for a 40B model, with released data and code to replicate.

results.title: Scaling the Tülu 3 post-training recipes to surpass DeepSeek V3 (Ai2)
results.snippet: Shows the Tülu 3 SFT→DPO→RLVR recipe scaling to 405B and beating DeepSeek V3, with infra details (16-way TP vLLM inference, 240 GPUs for training) — concrete evidence that this open post-training stack rivals frontier models, relevant to a 40B India-first model targeting Gemma-class quality.

results.title: Post-Training in 2026: GRPO, DAPO, RLVR & Beyond
results.snippet: 2026 survey of the current modular post-training stack (Instruction SFT → Thinking SFT → DPO/IPO → RLVR/GRPO) citing DeepSeek-R1, Nemotron 3 Super, OLMo 3; covers RLVR for verifiable code/tool-use rewards, GRPO as critic-free policy update, and the newest agentic frontier requiring interactive RL environments (NeMo Gym) — directly maps the coding/agentic RL methods that distinguish strong models.

results.title: Post-Training of Large Language Models — Georgia Tech CS 7643 (lecture notes)
results.snippet: Academic overview tying together SFT (LIMA 1,000-example quality-over-quantity finding), DPO's closed-form implicit reward, RLVR, GRPO, and RLAIF (RLAIF≈RLHF on summarization) — useful structured reference for justifying data-quality and method choices in the post-training design.

results.title: Viewing LLM Post-Training through the Lens of Teacher Signals
results.snippet: Explicitly addresses agentic tool-use data: recommends capturing intermediate traces (tool calls, decision/correction steps), not just final success/failure, to overcome sparse reward, and matching teacher signal (SFT vs DPO vs GRPO) to failure mode — practical guidance for building agentic tool-use SFT/RL data.

results.title: Awesome-LLM-Post-training (MBZUAI) — Reasoning/RL survey & resource list
results.snippet: Curated index of post-training papers, datasets, and RL-for-reasoning resources (SFT, DPO, GRPO, RLVR, agentic) — a jump-off point to primary sources and preference/tool-use datasets for building the alignment data recipe.

results.title: The FineWeb Datasets: Decanting the Web for the Finest Text Data at Scale
results.snippet: Primary source (arXiv) for the full cleaning stack: MinHash LSH dedup (5-grams, 112 hashes, 14 buckets of 8, ~75% Jaccard threshold), per-snapshot vs global dedup ablation, C4+custom heuristic filters (~22% tokens removed), and >70 released ablation models. Directly grounds dedup/quality-filtering design decisions for a 40B pretraining recipe.

results.title: The FineWeb Datasets (NeurIPS 2024 Datasets & Benchmarks Track)
results.snippet: Peer-reviewed PDF of the FineWeb paper — the citable primary source for dedup parameters, empirical data-ablation methodology, and FineWeb-Edu classifier results (MMLU 33%->37%, ARC 46%->57%). Best canonical citation for the evidence base.

results.title: FineWeb-Edu: Quality Educational Web Data
results.snippet: Focuses on the model-based educational quality classifier (1.3T subset). Key ablation number: FineWeb-Edu matches other corpora on MMLU with ~10x fewer tokens, and beats RefinedWeb by 4-8 pts at fixed compute — direct evidence for quality-classifier value in a token-budget-constrained recipe.

results.title: AI Pretraining Data Curation on GPU Cloud: NeMo Curator, Datatrove, and FineWeb-Style Pipelines (2026 Guide)
results.snippet: End-to-end operational view of the cleaning stack including PII redaction (emails/phones/SSNs/IPs via regex+NER) and 13-gram bloom-filter benchmark decontamination — the two stages the FineWeb paper covers less. Also gives pipeline yield (~5-7% pass rate) and dedup compute costs relevant to a 40B run.

results.title: A Guide to the FineWeb2 Dataset: How It's Built, Filtered, and Used for Training LLMs
results.snippet: Covers FineWeb2's multilingual dedup change (global per-language dedup with minhash_cluster_size rehydration signal) — directly relevant to cleaning Indic-language corpora and quality-weighting via dedup metadata for an India-first model.

results.title: Papers Explained 174: FineWeb
results.snippet: Concise secondary walkthrough of the FineWeb pipeline stages and ablation findings (trafilatura extraction, custom line/punctuation filters, per-snapshot dedup rationale). Useful quick reference but subordinate to the arXiv/NeurIPS primary sources.

claims.quote: GRPO ... "eliminates the critic entirely," sampling 8–64 responses; advantage = "(reward_i - mean) / std." Introduced in DeepSeekMath, used in DeepSeek-R1.

claims.claim: DAPO (ByteDance/Tsinghua, 2025) uses four techniques (Clip-Higher, Dynamic Sampling, Token-level Policy Gradient Loss, Overlong Reward Shaping) and trained Qwen2.5-32B to 50 points on AIME 2024, outperforming DeepSeek-R1-Zero with 50% fewer training steps.
claims.quote: On AIME 2024, trained Qwen2.5-32B "to 50 points, outperforming DeepSeek-R1-Zero with 50% fewer training steps." Open-sourced.

claims.claim: RLVR (Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards), as shown by DeepSeek-R1, can produce emergent reasoning using rewards from unit tests, proof checkers, and math verifiers without human annotators.
claims.quote: DeepSeek-R1 showed "pure RL with verifiable rewards (RLVR) can produce emergent reasoning capabilities." Reward comes from unit tests, proof checkers, math verifiers — no human annotators.

claims.claim: Agentic tool-use post-training at scale: NVIDIA's Nemotron 3 Super was trained with NeMo Gym across 21 environment configurations generating 1.2 million rollouts, and used 7M SFT samples from a 40M corpus.
claims.quote: NeMo Gym (NVIDIA): Nemotron 3 Super trained "across 21 environment configurations generating 1.2 million rollouts." ... Nemotron 3 Super reportedly used 7M samples from a 40M corpus.

claims.claim: Reference-free preference optimization methods improve over DPO: SimPO removes the reference model and claims +6.4 points on AlpacaEval 2 and +7.5 points on Arena-Hard.
claims.quote: SimPO: removes the reference model; claimed "+6.4 points on AlpacaEval 2" and "7.5 points on Arena-Hard."

claims.quote: We pre-train Llama 3 on a corpus of about 15T multilingual tokens, compared to 1.8T tokens for Llama 2.

claims.claim: Llama 3's final pretraining data mix is ~50% general knowledge, 25% math/reasoning, 17% code, and 8% multilingual tokens — a directly usable data-recipe percentage breakdown.
claims.quote: roughly 50% of tokens corresponding to general knowledge, 25% of mathematical and reasoning tokens, 17% code tokens, and 8% multilingual tokens

claims.claim: Llama 3 uses a 128K-token vocabulary that improves English compression from 3.17 to 3.94 characters per token — a concrete tokenizer vocab-size and fertility/compression datapoint.
claims.quote: We use a vocabulary with 128K tokens... our new tokenizer improves compression rates on a sample of English data from 3.17 to 3.94 characters per token

claims.claim: Data cleaning combined multi-level dedup (URL, document, line) with global MinHash near-duplicate removal, line-frequency filtering (>6 occurrences per 30M-doc bucket), PII/unsafe-content filters, and model-based quality classifiers (fastText, RoBERTa).
claims.quote: We perform global MinHash de-duplication across the entire dataset to remove near duplicate documents... We remove lines that appeared more than 6 times in each bucket of 30M documents.

claims.claim: Post-training used a simple pipeline of supervised finetuning (SFT), rejection sampling (RS), and Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) applied over multiple rounds — a reference alignment recipe.
claims.quote: a relatively simple post-training procedure based on supervised finetuning (SFT), rejection sampling (RS), and direct preference optimization (DPO

claims.quote: FineWeb: 15-trillion tokens from 96 Common Crawl snapshots ... FineWeb-Edu: 1.3-trillion tokens of educational content

claims.quote: Used 5-grams, 112 hash functions, "split into 14 buckets of 8 hashes each — targeting documents that are at least 75% similar"

claims.quote: Global dedup provided "only a modest performance uplift"; per-snapshot dedup "matched RefinedWeb's performance" ... On oldest snapshots global dedup "removed as much as 90% of the original base filtered data"

claims.claim: The FineWeb-Edu quality classifier used Llama-3-70B-Instruct to score 460,000 samples on a 0-5 educational scale, trained a linear regression on Snowflake-arctic-embed-m embeddings (threshold 3, F1 82%), and classifying the full 15T tokens took 6,000 H100 GPU hours.

claims.quote: DeepSeek-V3 requires only 2.788M H800 GPU hours for its full training

claims.quote: we distill the reasoning capability from the DeepSeek-R1 series of models

claims.claim: DeepSeek-V3 scores 88.5 on MMLU, 75.9 on MMLU-Pro, and 59.1 on GPQA, and is described as a top performer on the LiveCodeBench coding benchmark and MATH-500.
claims.quote: 88.5 on MMLU, 75.9 on MMLU-Pro, and 59.1 on GPQA

claims.claim: DeepSeek-V3 uses an auxiliary-loss-free load-balancing strategy and a multi-token prediction training objective as architectural/training innovations.
claims.quote: pioneers an auxiliary-loss-free strategy for load balancing ... sets a multi-token prediction training objective

claims.claim: FineWeb-Edu comprises 1.3 trillion tokens, derived by filtering the larger 15-trillion-token FineWeb corpus (96 Common Crawl snapshots) down by removing ~90% of raw data.
claims.quote: a high-quality, large-scale educational web dataset comprising 1.3 trillion tokens... removing ≈90% of raw data.

claims.claim: FineWeb-Edu's quality filter is a linear regressor on Snowflake-arctic-embed-m embeddings predicting a 0-5 educational score, trained on 460,000 candidates annotated by Llama-3-70B-Instruct; documents scoring >=3 are retained.
claims.quote: Llama-3-70B-Instruct annotates 460,000 candidates with additive scoring... A linear regressor, built on Snowflake-arctic-embed-m embeddings, predicts an educational score (0–5)... Documents with scores ≥3 are retained.

claims.quote: extracting 5-grams and using 112 hash functions split into 14 buckets (8 hashes each)... Documents with ≥75% similarity are considered duplicates.

claims.claim: Quality filtering yields large benchmark gains: MMLU improves from 33% to ~37% and ARC from 46% to 57% (+24%); a 1.82B model on 350B FineWeb-Edu tokens outperforms models trained on the full FineWeb, MassiveText, and Dolma.
claims.quote: improve from 33% to approximately 37% accuracy... performance jumps from 46% to 57% (+24%)... a 1.82B model trained on 350B FineWeb-Edu tokens outperforms models trained on the entire FineWeb

claims.quote: Uses the trafilatura library for HTML-to-text conversion... fastText English identification with "confidence ≥ 0.65."

claims.quote: we first introduce FineWeb, a 15-trillion token dataset of text sourced from 96 Common Crawl snapshots... Both datasets are released under the permissive ODC-By License.

result.evidence: The claim is verbatim-supported by the primary Gemma 3 Technical Report (arXiv 2503.19786 / DeepMind PDF), which states "we train on 14T tokens for Gemma 3 27B, 12T for the 12B version, 4T for the 4B, and 2T tokens for the 1B." This is independently corroborated by Google's developer blog ("2T tokens for 1B, 4T for 4B, 12T for 12B, and 14T tokens for 27B") and the official Gemma 3 model card (ai.google.dev), which restates identical figures and adds the later 270M variant (6T). No contradicting source found. Source is a primary technical report; claim strength matches source quality. The only minor nuance: the report attributes the token increase over Gemma 2 to the image/text mix and expanded multilingual data, not to pure scaling — but this does not affect the numeric claim.

The claim is a direct, faithful restatement of the primary source. The Gemma 3 Technical Report (Google DeepMind, 2025-03-12; also arXiv:2503.19786) states verbatim: "we train on 14T tokens for Gemma 3 27B, 12T for the 12B version, 4T for the 4B, and 2T tokens for the 1B." The claim maps each budget to each size exactly (27B=14T, 12B=12T, 4B=4T, 1B=2T) with no overreach. Corroborated independently by the arXiv HTML version and multiple third-party summaries (HuggingFace blog, learnopencv, Medium write-ups), all citing identical figures. Source is the primary technical report — quality matches claim strength. Current (Gemma 3 released March 2025). Not a marketing/cherry-picked claim; it is a factual training-config disclosure. One minor caveat: the report frames these as approximate/"slightly larger than Gemma 2" budgets, but the specific numbers are explicit.

The claim is a direct paraphrase of the Gemma 3 Technical Report (primary source, Google DeepMind), which states verbatim: "We use the same tokenizer as Gemini 2.0: a SentencePiece tokenizer with split digits, preserved whitespace, and byte-level encodings (Kudo and Richardson, 2018). The resulting vocabulary has 262k entries. This tokenizer is more balanced for non-English languages." Every element of the claim (same tokenizer as Gemini 2.0, SentencePiece, split digits, preserved whitespace, byte-level encodings, 262k vocab, more balanced for non-English) maps 1:1 to the quote with no overreach. Corroborated by independent secondary sources: arXiv HTML mirror of the report (arxiv.org/html/2503.19786v1), Google Developers Blog ("gemma-explained-whats-new-in-gemma-3"), and multiple technical write-ups, all confirming 262k SentencePiece, split digits, preserved whitespace, byte-level, up from 256k in Gemma 2. result.summary: For a 40B "India-first" LLM, the evidence base points to a clear recipe. Token budgets for 27-40B open models cluster at 14-18T tokens (Gemma 3 27B: 14T; Qwen2.5: 18T; DeepSeek-V3: 14.8T; Llama 3: ~15T), and Llama 3's published mix (~50% general, 25% math/reasoning, 17% code, 8% multilingual) is the most directly usable data-recipe breakdown — though for Indic excellence the multilingual share must be raised well above 8%. Indic pretraining data is anchored by AI4Bharat's Sangraha (251B tokens, 22 languages, but ~65% synthetic), IndicCorp v2 (20.9B tokens, 24 languages), plus FineWeb-2 and OCR/transcription pipelines; native high-quality Indic web text remains scarce and skewed (Hindi ~1.86B vs Assamese ~32.6M in v1). Cleaning best practice combines multi-level + global MinHash dedup (FineWeb: 5-grams, 112 hashes, 14×8 buckets, 75% threshold), LLM-scored educational quality classifiers (FineWeb-Edu: Llama-3-70B labels → embedding regression, filtered 15T→1.3T), and PII/safety filtering — with the caveat that global dedup showed diminishing/negative returns. Post-training converges on SFT + RL, with GRPO and rule-based+model-based rewards (DeepSeek-V3, no DPO) and R1-style reasoning distillation. On tokenizers, large vocabularies (Gemma 3: 262K; Llama 3: 128K) improve non-English/compression balance but carry an embedding-parameter cost that becomes negligible at 40B scale (~1.4B/27B ≈ 5%), favoring a large, Indic-balanced vocab.

findings.claim: Token budgets for 27-40B-class open frontier models cluster tightly at ~14-18 trillion tokens, giving a defensible target range for a 40B model.
findings.evidence: Gemma 3 27B: 14T tokens (12B=12T, 4B=4T, 1B=2T), scaling budget with size. Llama 3: ~15T (405B flagship = 15.6T), an 8.3x jump over Llama 2's 1.8T. Qwen2.5: 18T (up from 7T in Qwen2). DeepSeek-V3: 14.8T (671B MoE, 37B active/token). A 40B dense model should plan for the upper end of this range (15-18T+).

findings.claim: Llama 3's final pretraining mix (~50% general knowledge, 25% math/reasoning, 17% code, 8% multilingual) is the most concrete published data-recipe breakdown; an India-first coding model should raise multilingual and hold/raise code+math.
findings.evidence: Llama 3 report gives exact end-state percentages over ~15T tokens, with proportions dynamically adjusted during training (upsampled math, increased non-English late, downsampled low-quality). This is a snapshot of the final mix, not a static recipe. For India-first coding/agentic goals, the 8% multilingual share is a floor to exceed and the 17% code / 25% math shares are the reference for strong coding/reasoning.

findings.claim: AI4Bharat's Sangraha (251B tokens, 22 languages) is the largest cleaned Indic pretraining corpus, but ~65% (162B) is synthetic (translated/romanized Wikimedia), not native web text.
findings.evidence: Sangraha = Verified (64B: scraped human-verified sites + OCR of Indic PDFs + transcribed audio/video) + Unverified (24B: perplexity-filtered from CulturaX/MADLAD-400 via n-gram LMs trained on Verified, extending CCNet) + Synthetic (162B: Wikimedia EN translated into 14 Indic langs via IndicTrans2, then romanized via IndicXlit). Peer-reviewed (Khan et al., ACL 2024, arXiv:2403.06350), CC-BY-4.0. The heavy synthetic share is a data-quality caveat for a frontier recipe.

findings.claim: IndicCorp v2 (20.9B tokens, 24 languages, 4 families) and the older AI4Bharat-IndicNLP corpus (2.7B words, 10 languages) are the primary native monolingual Indic resources, alongside FineWeb-2 — but Indic data is small and severely skewed by language.
findings.evidence: IndicCorp v2: 20.9B tokens, 24 langs, 4 families, 2.3x/+12 langs over v1 (Doddapaneni et al., ACL 2023). AI4Bharat-IndicNLP: 2.7B words, 10 langs, Indo-Aryan+Dravidian (Kunchukuttan et al. 2020). Per-language skew is severe: IndicCorp v1 Hindi 1.86B tokens vs Assamese 32.6M (~57x gap). AI4Bharat's own IndicBERT-v3 corpus explicitly drew from Sangraha-Verified, HuggingFaceFW/fineweb-2, and IndicCorpV2 among others — a concrete source list to mirror. Native Indic web text remains scarce relative to frontier budgets.

findings.claim: A phased/curriculum sampling schedule with fixed language-family ratios is a documented technique for balancing English foundation against high- and low-resource Indic languages.
findings.evidence: AI4Bharat IndicBERT-v3-4B used a four-phase curriculum: Phase 1 English 0.30, Phase 2 (14 high/mid-resource Indic) 0.25, Phase 3 (8 low-resource) 0.15, Phase 4 (joint consolidation, all 23) 0.25, with the final ~10% of steps for joint consolidation to mitigate catastrophic forgetting. IMPORTANT: this is a 4B bidirectional ENCODER (Gemma-3-4b-pt base, ~35B tokens), not a 40B from-scratch decoder — the ratios are illustrative of curriculum design, not directly a frontier decoder recipe. Ratios are per-phase sampling weights (sum 0.95), not a single corpus partition.

findings.claim: Large-scale cleaning should combine multi-level + global MinHash dedup, line-frequency filtering, PII/safety filters, and model-based quality classifiers.
findings.evidence: Llama 3: URL/document/line-level dedup + global MinHash near-dup removal + line-frequency filter (drop lines appearing >6x per 30M-doc bucket) + dirty-word/PII/unsafe filtering + fastText and RoBERTa/DistilRoBERTa quality classifiers. FineWeb specifies MinHash params: 5-grams, 112 hash functions in 14 buckets of 8, targeting ≥75% similarity.

findings.claim: LLM-scored educational quality classifiers (FineWeb-Edu style) are a proven, cheap way to filter web-scale corpora, and can be replicated for Indic.
findings.evidence: FineWeb is 15T tokens from 96 Common Crawl snapshots; FineWeb-Edu is 1.3T filtered via a classifier: Llama-3-70B-Instruct scored 460K samples 0-5, a linear regression on frozen Snowflake-arctic-embed-m embeddings (threshold 3, F1 82%) then classified all 15T tokens in ~6,000 H100 GPU-hours (~92% of tokens removed). This is a directly transferable pipeline for building an Indic-Edu quality filter.

findings.claim: More deduplication is not always better — global dedup can hurt, so dedup strategy needs tuning.
findings.evidence: FineWeb: per-snapshot (individual) dedup matched RefinedWeb performance, while global dedup gave only a modest uplift and removed up to 90% of base-filtered data on older snapshots — the retained old-crawl data was of worse quality than what was removed. None of the attempted dedup methods outperformed individual dedup. Relevant for scarce Indic data where over-aggressive global dedup could strip valuable text.

findings.claim: Post-training should use SFT + RL with GRPO, combining rule-based (verifiable math/code) and model-based reward models, plus reasoning distillation from a strong R1-style teacher; DPO is not required.
findings.evidence: DeepSeek-V3 (671B MoE, 37B active, 14.8T pretraining tokens) post-trains with SFT then RL via GRPO (no value model), using rule-based rewards for verifiable tasks and model-based rewards for free-form answers, and distills reasoning from the DeepSeek-R1 series (1.5M SFT instances). No DPO is used. This gives a concrete RLVR/distillation template for a coding/agentic + Indic model.

findings.claim: A large, non-English-balanced tokenizer vocabulary (200K+) is favored for an Indic model, and its embedding-parameter cost becomes negligible at 40B scale.
findings.evidence: Gemma 3 uses a 262K-entry SentencePiece tokenizer (same as Gemini 2.0; split digits, preserved whitespace, byte-level) explicitly 'more balanced for non-English languages.' Embedding cost shrinks with scale: 302M of the 1B model (~30%) vs 1,416M of the 27B model (~5%, with 25,600M non-embedding) — so a large Indic-balanced vocab is nearly free at 40B. Llama 3's 128K vocab improved English compression 3.17→3.94 chars/token, showing vocab design directly affects fertility/compression.

result.caveats: Time-sensitivity: token budgets and recipes move fast — Qwen3 already doubled Qwen2.5's corpus to 36T, so the 14-18T range is a 2024/early-2025 snapshot and the practical target is likely rising. Data-recipe percentages: only Llama 3 publishes an explicit mix; Gemma 3, Qwen2.5, and DeepSeek-V3 do NOT disclose comparable code/math/multilingual splits, so the recipe generalization rests substantially on one source. Indic data quality: Sangraha's 251B headline is ~65% synthetic (machine-translated/romanized), and its 'largest/high-quality' framing is AI4Bharat's self-description; native high-quality Indic web text is far smaller and severely language-skewed. The IndicBERT-v3 four-phase curriculum (Finding 5) comes from a 4B bidirectional ENCODER trained on ~35B tokens, not a 40B from-scratch decoder — transferability to frontier decoder pretraining is limited. No primary-source numbers were surfaced here for several items named in the question: Sarvam-1 (68K vocab), Krutrim, IndicSuperTokenizer, Bhasha-wiki, Indic per-script fertility (tokens/word) tables, or the specific Indic evaluation benchmarks (MILU, IndicGenBench, IndicMMLU-Pro), coding/agentic benchmarks (LiveCodeBench, SWE-bench, Terminal-Bench, BFCL, tau-bench), and whether Indic coding/agentic benchmarks exist — the verified claim set did not cover these, so they remain gaps. 'Fertility' vs 'compression': Llama 3's 3.17→3.94 is chars/token (higher=better compression), the inverse of fertility (tokens/word); do not conflate. No independent evidence for 'diminishing returns above ~200K vocab' was among the verified claims — only the embedding-cost-shrinks-with-scale point is confirmed.
openQuestions: What are the concrete Indic tokenizer fertility (tokens/word) numbers per script (Devanagari, Tamil, Telugu, Bengali, etc.) and for code, and how do Sarvam-1 (68K), IndicSuperTokenizer, Gemma-3 (262K), Llama/Qwen/DeepSeek vocabularies compare on Indic fertility? Is there real evidence of diminishing returns above ~200K vocab?

Do dedicated Indic coding and agentic/tool-use benchmarks exist, or must a 40B India-first coding model be evaluated only on English-centric HumanEval/MBPP/LiveCodeBench/SWE-bench/BFCL/tau-bench plus separate Indic language benchmarks (MILU, IndicGenBench, IndicMMLU-Pro, Indic-QA)?

What are the actual SFT/preference/agentic-trace data sources and volumes for Indic instruction-following, Hinglish/transliteration, and India-first cultural alignment (Sarvam, Krutrim pipelines) — the verified claims covered pretraining data far more than post-training data?

What code/math/multilingual mix percentages did Gemma 3, Qwen2.5, and DeepSeek-V3 actually use, given only Llama 3 disclosed an explicit breakdown, and how should the multilingual share be sized for an India-first model without eroding coding/math performance?
